strengths: The paper identifies and successfully addresses two critical bottlenecks of current 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) open-vocabulary pipelines: spatial ambiguity (semantic bleeding) due to unstructured overlapping geometry, and multi-level semantic ambiguity from hierarchical SAM-based pipelines.

The transition to a structured Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) backbone enables deterministic, confidence-aware 3D feature fusion and avoids the heavy memory bottleneck of inverse volume rendering on unstructured Gaussians, enabling O(1) memory scalability.
The proposed multi-level TSDF depth confidence mechanism provides a robust view-consistency weight, which significantly cleans up feature projection and boundary delineation.

The use of the agglomerative AM-RADIO model bypasses expensive hierarchical SAM mask extraction, reducing data preprocessing time drastically from ~120 minutes to ~14 minutes, while achieving state-of-the-art results on fine-grained and multi-scale queries.
Highly impressive quantitative results on ScanNet (e.g., +21.56% mIoU improvement over Dr. Splat on 19 classes) and LERF 3D object retrieval, accompanied by thorough ablation studies.
weaknesses: While the system is highly effective, the technical novelty of several components is somewhat incremental, as it combines SVRaster, depth/normal regularization from prior works, AM-RADIO, and upsampling modules (SCRA/SCGA) from RADSeg.

In 2D object retrieval (Table 2), the proposed method shows slightly lower performance in average mIoU (56.84%) compared to LangSplatV2 (59.88%), though it is still highly competitive and excels on the complex 'ramen' scene.
There are minor presentation issues, such as typographical errors in the figures (e.g., 'Unders at nd ni g' in Fig. 1, 'Sliglip2' vs 'Siglip2' in Fig. 2, and 'groud truth' in Fig. 10 caption).

strengths: Well-Motivated Core Idea: Shifting from unstructured, overlapping 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to an explicit Sparse Voxel representation (SVRaster) is a logical and highly effective solution to the spatial ambiguity and semantic bleeding issues common in direct feature lifting.

Efficient and Scalable Fusion: By leveraging disjoint voxels, the feature projection can be executed in isolated spatial batches with O(1) memory, addressing the severe system memory bottlenecks of prior 3DGS-based feature registration methods.

Robust Geometry and Semantic Priors: The combination of monocular depth/normal regularizations with the multi-level TSDF depth confidence map provides a robust geometric backbone, while the integration of the agglomerative AM-RADIO model bypasses complex, multi-stage 2D mask-pooling pipelines (like SAM).

Outstanding Empirical Performance: The proposed LESV demonstrates remarkable improvements over existing SOTA methods on both LERF and ScanNet benchmarks, achieving a substantial margin (e.g., +21.5% mIoU on ScanNet 19-class point cloud segmentation) while drastically accelerating data preprocessing and feature-lifting times (to ~3 minutes).

Thorough Analysis and Ablation: The paper and its supplementary material provide detailed ablation studies, algorithm pseudocode, and qualitative verification of downstream capabilities such as open-vocabulary autonomous driving segmentation and 3D scene editing.
weaknesses: Dependence on Monocular Priors: The visual and geometric consistency of the framework relies heavily on monocular depth and normal estimation networks. The paper would benefit from a discussion on how the pipeline behaves in complex, highly reflective, or textureless scenes where such monocular priors frequently fail.

Voxel Grid Memory Footprint: While the feature fusion memory is optimized via spatial batching, storing high-dimensional features inside high-resolution voxels can still pose a significant memory footprint during inference or rendering. A quantitative discussion of the voxel grid's final memory consumption would be helpful.

Clarity and Minor Typos: On page 12, under 'Qualitative Analysis', there is a broken figure reference ('we provide visual comparisons... in Figure ??.'). This should be corrected to point to the correct figure (presumably Fig. 10).

strengths: The transition from unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) is well-motivated, successfully addressing spatial ambiguities and semantic bleeding near object boundaries.

Significant efficiency improvements in preprocessing (reducing time from over 2 hours to 14 minutes) and feature lifting (down to ~3 minutes) by leveraging the multi-scale features of the AM-RADIO foundation model without per-scene SAM mask generation.
Strong quantitative results on 3D object retrieval (LERF) and 3D point cloud understanding (ScanNet), showing a massive improvement in mIoU over the baseline registration method Dr. Splat.
Extensive ablation studies and qualitative visualizations demonstrating practical downstream applications such as scene editing and autonomous driving.
weaknesses: Low methodological novelty: Almost all core components of the pipeline are directly borrowed or adapted from existing literature (SVRaster for geometry, DNGaussian for patch depth, MonoSDF for normals, AM-RADIO for semantic features, RADSeg for SCRA/SCGA attention, and J-Neus for TSDF fusion). The overall contribution is more of an engineering integration than a fundamentally new concept.

Underperformance on 2D object retrieval: As shown in Table 2, the proposed method is outperformed by LangSplatV2 (56.84% mIoU vs. 59.88% mIoU). While the authors attribute this to not being optimized for 2D, it represents a clear performance trade-off compared to state-of-the-art distillation methods.

Unfair/Unclear baseline comparisons on ScanNet: In Table 3, the proposed method shows a massive jump (+21% mIoU) over Dr. Splat. However, SVRaster has a structured grid which inherently facilitates local neighborhood queries (K=8 nearest voxels), whereas 3DGS requires more complex mapping (K=64 nearest Gaussians). It is unclear how much of this performance gain comes from the voxel representation's structural advantage in point cloud feature transfer versus the actual proposed fusion methodology.

Heavy reliance on a specific foundation model: The framework's ability to resolve multi-level semantic ambiguity is entirely offloaded to the pre-trained AM-RADIO model. There is no analysis of how the system would generalize to other widely-used open-vocabulary models (e.g., standard CLIP or SigLIP) if AM-RADIO is unavailable or replaced.

strengths: The paper identifies key limitations in current 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) open-vocabulary methods, namely spatial ambiguity from unstructured geometry and multi-level semantic ambiguity from hierarchical SAM-based mask pooling, and addresses them effectively.

The proposed transition to Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) enables deterministic, confidence-aware feature registration, which significantly reduces semantic bleeding and ray-like spillovers compared to 3DGS.

The introduction of the multi-level TSDF confidence-weighted fusion and monocular priors (depth and normal) successfully regularizes the voxel geometry, addressing the 'hollow' geometry problem of vanilla SVRaster.

The integration of the AM-RADIO foundation model with a self-correcting sliding window upsampling strategy allows the method to achieve fine-grained multi-scale querying with low computational overhead and without multi-level SAM mask extraction.

Outstanding performance on the ScanNet open-vocabulary 3D semantic segmentation benchmark, showing a substantial improvement (+21.56% mIoU on 19 classes) over previous state-of-the-art registration methods like Dr. Splat, along with competitive results on LERF 2D/3D object retrieval.
weaknesses: The solution to multi-level semantic ambiguity is heavily reliant on existing, pre-trained heavy vision foundation models (AM-RADIO) and upsampling/aggregation techniques borrowed from RADSeg, which limits the algorithmic novelty of the semantic representation itself.

As discussed in the limitations, the upsampled feature maps are constrained to a relatively low resolution (256x256), leading to slightly inferior performance compared to Dr. Splat on scenes with small or dense objects (e.g., 'figurines' and 'waldo_kitchen' in Table 1).

Unlike some 3DGS-based language fields, the proposed sparse voxel representation does not support high-fidelity, real-time novel-view rendering of semantic features, restricting its applicability for interactive real-time visualization.

strengths: Well-motivated transition from unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to structured Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) to address spatial and semantic bleeding/ambiguity in 3D open-vocabulary scene understanding.
The proposed geometric-aware robust volume fusion using multi-level TSDF confidence effectively aligns features near the surface and handles view-dependent inconsistencies.

Leveraging the emergent dense alignment properties of AM-RADIO allows the framework to capture multi-level semantics without expensive SAM-based hierarchical mask pooling, reducing preprocessing times significantly (from ~120 mins to ~14 mins).

Outstanding experimental results, especially on the ScanNet point cloud understanding benchmark, outperforming existing baselines by a large margin (+21.56% mIoU on the 19-class split) while showing competitive performance on LERF retrieval and localization.
Comprehensive qualitative and quantitative evaluation, including detailed ablation studies, memory usage analysis, and extended applications like scene editing and autonomous driving scenarios.
weaknesses: Resolution bottleneck of upsampled features: As acknowledged by the authors, the upsampled Vision Foundation Model (VFM) features are limited to 256, which is lower than SAM masks and degrades performance on highly detailed or densely packed scenes (e.g., the figurines scene).

Dependency on monocular priors: The geometry and final volume fusion accuracy heavily rely on the quality of monocular depth and normal priors, which may fail in complex structures, challenging lighting, or highly reflective surfaces.
Unlike distillation-based methods, direct feature registration methods like LESV do not natively support real-time high-fidelity novel-view feature rendering.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated shift from unstructured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) to Sparse Voxel Rasterization (SVRaster) to address spatial ambiguity, semantic bleeding, and global depth-sorting memory bottlenecks.

Substantial improvements in 3D open-vocabulary point cloud understanding on ScanNet, outperforming the state-of-the-art Dr. Splat baseline by +21.56% mIoU on ScanNet-19 and showing strong generalization across 10-class and 15-class setups.

High computational and memory efficiency: bounded peak memory (around 25 GB compared to over 130 GB for Dr. Splat) and drastically minimized per-scene preprocessing time (~14 minutes compared to ~120 minutes of prior works).

Thorough ablation studies (Tables 4, 5, and 8) that successfully isolate the performance gains from the geometric priors, the TSDF-based confidence gating, the upsampling strategy, and the choice of the AM-RADIO vision-language foundation model backbone.
weaknesses: The exact monocular depth and normal estimation model used as the 2D prior for geometric refinement is not clearly specified in the main text (only through reference to [15, 33]), which limits immediate reproducibility without scanning the citations or supplementary materials.

While the proposed sliding-window upsampling with SCRA & SCGA is thoroughly evaluated in Table 8, the overall spatial resolution is still bottlenecked at 256. This leads to slightly lower performance compared to mask-proposal methods on highly dense or fine-grained scenes, such as the 'figurines' scene in LERF.

Like most direct registration methods, it does not support real-time rendering of high-fidelity language fields for novel-view synthesis, representing a trade-off between 3D-native querying precision and rendering quality.
